title: Grounding techniques explained
citation: Frausing, K. P., Flammild, M. H., & Dahlgaard, J. (2025). Mind-Body Practices for Mental Health in Higher Education: Breathing, Grounding, and Consistency Are Essential for Stress and Anxiety Management. Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland), 13(16), 2049.
content:
Grounding techniques explained.

Grounding techniques are simple strategies that help bring your attention back to the present moment when your thoughts, emotions, or physical sensations feel overwhelming. They work by shifting your focus away from distressing internal experiences and towards what is happening around you right now. Grounding helps you feel more settled and able to respond rather than react.

Isn't grounding just a distraction, not a real fix?

Grounding is often misunderstood as a way of avoiding emotions or pretending they do not exist. In reality, grounding helps calm the nervous system so you can feel more present and think more clearly. Once you feel more settled, it is often easier to understand, process and cope with whatever is causing the distress.

Why does grounding help when I feel overwhelmed or disconnected?

When people become highly stressed, anxious, or emotionally overwhelmed, the brain can become focused on perceived danger while the body stays in a heightened state of alert. Some people may also feel disconnected from themselves or their surroundings. Grounding interrupts this cycle by directing attention towards the present through the senses, breathing, movement, or the environment. This helps the brain recognise that you are safe in the current moment, allowing the nervous system to begin settling.

Types of grounding techniques.

Grounding can take many forms because different approaches work for different people. Physical grounding involves noticing sensations in your body, such as feeling your feet against the floor, holding a cool object, or taking slow breaths. Mental grounding involves focusing your attention on facts around you, such as naming five things you can see or counting backwards. Soothing grounding uses comforting experiences, such as listening to calming sounds, repeating reassuring statements, or imagining a safe place. Having several techniques available makes it easier to find one that works in different situations.

Grounding vs avoidance: what's the difference?

Grounding and avoidance may look similar because both shift your attention away from distress in the moment, but they serve different purposes. Grounding is a temporary way of helping your mind and body become calmer so that you can cope more effectively. Avoidance is trying to escape difficult thoughts, emotions, or situations altogether, often preventing them from being processed. Grounding supports emotional regulation, while avoidance often keeps distress going over time.

Why do I feel overwhelmed or disconnected?

Feeling overwhelmed or disconnected can happen when the brain and nervous system are under more stress than they can comfortably manage. Ongoing pressure, strong emotions, fatigue, trauma, or prolonged anxiety can make it harder to stay present. Some people notice they feel detached from themselves, emotionally numb, or as though everything around them feels unreal. These reactions are the nervous system's way of trying to cope with overwhelming experiences, even though they can feel confusing or unsettling.

When should I get help with grounding?

Grounding techniques are useful skills that many people can learn and practise on their own, but they are not always enough on their own. If you regularly feel overwhelmed, disconnected, or find that distress is interfering with your daily life despite using grounding strategies, it may be helpful to seek professional support. A mental health professional can help you understand what is contributing to these experiences and teach additional evidence-based strategies alongside grounding techniques.
